attempts.summary: Configured node1 (VyOS) as a transit router between lan-a (node2, 10.60.0.0/24 on eth1) and lan-b (node3, 10.60.1.0/24 on eth2), entirely via an Ansible playbook run from node4 (the control node with Ansible installed). No NAT/masquerade was configured, so original source addresses are preserved end-to-end; connectivity was proven on ICMP, SSH (22), and arbitrary TCP ports (5555, 6666) with tcpdump and HTTP server access logs confirming unmodified source IPs. Host firewalld on node2/node3 was opened via rich rules (in the same playbook) for the peer subnet since it was independently blocking non-allowlisted ports. The playbook is fully idempotent (second and later runs show changed=0 on all hosts). All 4 managed nodes (node1-node4) were then restarted one at a time via native reboot, boot_id changes were captured proving real restarts, and post-restart health/config/connectivity were re-verified for each. Note: node1's SSH key for the `vyos` user is regenerated from config.boot by VyOS's system_login.py reconciler on every boot, so the cluster key had to be committed via `set system login user vyos authentication public-keys` (native VyOS config) rather than left in the ephemeral authorized_keys file — this was necessary for Ansible SSH access to survive the restart and is not itself part of the lan-a/lan-b routing task.
